title: Hamilton Lake, the grandmother's cornet and learning Isham Jones solos on a slow victrola
summary: The lake pavilion owner asks for a trumpet player, his grandmother buys him a cornet on condition he play in Sunday school, and he learns Louis Panico's choruses off a victrola running slow, so all in the wrong key.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Well, tell us about getting the horn and the playing in the Sunday school band--

Well, of course, first I went to-- the band got a job at a lake in the Summertime and I went up to a lake called Hamilton Lake, Indiana and I played that whole summer up there and we were -- the band was just very popular; everybody loved the band and, mind you now, we were just kids and we were pounding out some pretty darn good dance music for that time. And, of course, we used to all wait in line when the records would come in the shop so we could hear Ted Lewis, Isham Jones and that's the only jazz we heard. So, we didn't know whether we were playing jazz right or not. We were just seeing if we could make it sound something like those records, you know. So, at the end of that summer, the man that runs the pavillion up there - he said - "Listen, I'd love to have you guys back next year and, especially - Bill, do you want to come back - it's okay". But, he said - rather than have that banjo next year, I wish you could play the trumpet and if you could play the trumpet, next year, please do because if you can and you feel you can do it, because trumpets are now coming in the jazz band---
Well, cornet -- yes. Well, what--- I don't consider any difference too much. But, anyway,

I said - "Oh, please give me that chance. I'll do it. I'll do it, you know." So, uh, I got--- I had a grand-mother that was very religious on my father's side and, uh, I told her the story; she was the only chance I had to--- she had enough money for the cornet, I'm sure. So, I pleaded with her -- I said, if you just let me have enough money to buy a cornet, I promise I'll pay her back, but she said - "you don't have to pay me back". She said, "you know, we need a cornet in the Sunday school orchestra and if you promise me you'll play every Sunday in the Sunday school orchestra, I'll get you the horn." Of course, it wasn't a new one; it was an old Carl Fischer; it was an old one that we got in some shop there - somebody--- she knew somebody had one and she bought it from them; I don't know just how she got it. But, anyway, she got it and, uh, so that whole Wintertime, I got all these Isham Jones records I could find with Louie Panico on and I copied all his choruses by-- with a wind-up victrola. Now, not knowing that there was such a thing as the record running completely - 78 revolutions per minute, I didn't know about that so when I got through with all my copying all this stuff and I had it down to perfection and when the band got together--- I was playing it a little in the band once in awhile too -- our band and when we got ready to rehearse to go to the lake, I found out I had learned all the songs in the

wrong key (laughter), because the victrola was running slow. So, I had learned all those things in hard keys and flats - I don't know how. So, when I got back, when I got back to playing everything in the right key, it was just like learning all over again. It was a brand new ball game for me. I had to learn the fingering for all the songs that I had learned in the wrong key and it was very difficult, but I did go up there that summer playing the cornet and 50 - 50. I was playing the songs I know on the cornet and banjo on the others. And, of course, in those days, I sang a little. So, uh, I got by -- I got by that summer.
